title: Westbrook City Council — Special Meeting
note: This summary highlights the meeting's key discussions and decisions, with direct quotes and timestamps for verification — it is not a substitute for watching the full meeting. Summarization necessarily condenses and selects; for complete context, nuance, and anything not covered here, watch the full video at the link above. (Produced by: WestbrookCurrents.com)
attendance: Held remotely on Zoom. Present: President Jennifer Munro, Vice President Michael Shaughnessy, Brian McCambridge, Victor Chau, Anna Turcotte, Amy Faulkingham, Gary Rairdon (recorded absent for the votes at 1:04:38 and 1:06:33). Mayor David Morse also attended.

blocks.x: In Memoriam: Former Councilor John O'Hara
Remembering John O'Hara (21+ years of service through 2018, d. Feb. 13, 2026)

The meeting opened with an extended, unplanned tribute to former City Councilor John O'Hara. He died Feb. 13, 2026, after more than 21 years on the Council. Interim Director of Economic & Community Development Jerre Bryant, Councilors Turcotte, Chau, and Rairdon, and Mayor Morse each shared memories. O'Hara's legacy was connected to projects including the middle school, Anding Road, and the Green Fund.

“John brought a commitment and a level of energy to the legislative process in Westbrook that was genuine, was persistent. And agree or disagree with the point he was trying to make, he always put a smile on your face... Many members of the media have identified John over the years as the most quotable politician in the city of Westbrook.”
blocks.cite: Jerre Bryant, Interim Director of Economic & Community Development

blocks.x: Mayor's Message: Annual Project Updates (Robyn Saunders)

Project Manager Robyn Saunders gave her wide-ranging annual briefing on the City's major projects. She noted that roughly $7 million in outside grant funding has been brought to the five highlighted FY26 projects.

Landslide Vulnerability Assessment: the September 2020 landslide along Warren Avenue into the Presumpscot River prompted a state of emergency. After it, the City partnered with the University of Maine

College of Engineering and the Maine Geological Survey on a three-phase study of the Presumpscot clay formation responsible for regional landslide risk. Phase three is now underway with policy consultant Camoin Associates, Resilient Roots, and the University of Southern Maine Muskie School. It will produce a recommendation for a model ordinance (a city law) and overlay district (extra zoning rules for one area, added on top of the usual zoning). The rules would require extra geotechnical engineering (the study of soil and ground) in landslide-susceptible areas. The recommendation is expected within the year. (This is the same project as Order 2026-12, see below.)

Riverwalk North: a Brownfields cleanup and redevelopment project along the river's north bank. Brownfields are properties where past pollution can complicate reuse. An archaeological survey found no significant indigenous findings. Natural-resource constraints are pushing the trail alignment away from the river. This is in tension with abutters (neighbors whose land touches the site), who would prefer not to have the trail so close to their backyards. Negotiations with the Maine Department of Environmental Protection (DEP) and the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers are ongoing. The preliminary $8 million estimate is expected to change, since it is based on outdated 2015 design standards. A funding source transcribed as “Wick” provided $300,000 in starting money. That brought in another $4 million from the United States Environmental Protection Agency (USEPA). This leaves roughly a $3.7 million gap. Construction is expected around FY28.

Saccarappa Park: a $900,000 Brownfields Cleanup Award from the Maine Department of Economic and Community Development (DECD) is funding redevelopment of this downtown park. A revised cost estimate found a roughly $2 million gap for above-ground elements that Brownfields money can't cover. Construction is being phased and delayed into later 2026 to coordinate with the adjacent Kidder Street private development. That development is a $45+ million investment, with 1,200 linear feet of riverwalk boardwalk under a public easement (a right to use part of someone else's land). A separate $250,000 DECD grant will help clean up the connecting Mill Lane trail.

New Brownfields Assessment Program: a $500,000 USEPA award, with no local match, will fund a City-run program. The program will assess additional contaminated or underused properties. Credere Associates is the qualified environmental professional (see Order 2026-22).

Per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS) at Fraser Field/Warren Field/Westbrook High School: Maine DEP listed them as Tier IV PFAS sites in 2018. The City is using Greater Portland Council of Governments (GPCOG)'s Brownfields Assessment Grant to fund sampling. This is the same Memorandum of Understanding (a written agreement between two parties) previewed at the Feb. 2 meeting (see Order 2026-15). The Portland Water District is separately evaluating two of these same locations for a $15–20 million combined-sewer storage project. The timing of the two efforts will need to be coordinated.

Future projects (FY27+) include Riverwalk South lighting/security (~$600,000, pending Community Development Block Grant funding). They also include Westbrook Soccer Club field improvements (~$750,000). The Small Hardy Road field's owners have agreed to donate it to the City, with a spring 2026 dedication ceremony planned. Also planned are a $150,000 splash-pad feasibility study and beaver pond improvements.
Public Comment & Order 2026-16: Fire Training Facility CIP Deferral

Two Westbrook firefighters spoke during public comment. They urged the Council to reverse course on deferring Capital Improvement Plan (CIP) funding. The funding is for a long-planned regional fire training facility. It was developed jointly with the Westbrook Regional Vocational Center.

“On March 6, 2024, the City of Westbrook and the Westbrook Regional Vocational Center received $1.5 million in community project funding for the federal government to fund a fire training facility... If we keep delaying this project, not only will the cost rise, we may also risk losing this amazing opportunity. [It] would train the Westbrook Fire Department's 48 firefighters for over 800 hours... and train at least 20 new firefighters a year to help increase recruitment and retention in the area.”

Burchetto said a $150,000 FY26 soft-cost allocation was reduced to $50,000 and then deferred entirely to FY27. Firefighter Joe Carroll echoed the concern. He has worked on securing the project's federal earmark (money Congress sets aside for one project) since 2023 and travels regularly to Washington, D.C. on it. He noted that the project's regional and vocational-partnership angle was central to winning congressional support. He also noted that training out of town (currently in Yarmouth) costs the department significant overtime and apparatus wear.

During discussion of Order 2026-16, the first reading of the CIP (the first of two required votes), Councilor Rairdon raised the firefighters' concerns directly. He asked whether the deferral could be reconsidered, given the risk of losing the federal award. City Administrator Angela Holmes responded that the deferral reflects a due-diligence pause, not a cancellation. She said she believed the City is in year three of the federal grant's six-year spend-down window. The Fire Chief said the award came in 2023 but didn't know the exact date. Burchetto had dated it to March 2024. Holmes said the City wants to ensure the project proceeds correctly before committing further CIP funds in FY26. No amendment was offered.

Order 2026-16 (FY 2026 Capital Improvement Plan) passed first reading [1:17:43] unanimously, 7–0. Rairdon's concern is on the record but unresolved. The second and final reading, the final binding vote, was set for March 2. Moved by Gary Rairdon, seconded by Amy Faulkingham.
Orders of the Day — Second & Final Reading
Orders 2026-09, -10, -11, -12 — Emergency Repairs & Landslide Policy Services (Consent)

All four were first read at the Feb. 2, 2026 meeting. They cover gas meters ($20,607.85). They also cover Public Services heating, ventilation, and air conditioning (HVAC) ($43,688 + $11,350), and Walker Memorial Library HVAC ($43,636). The fourth is the Landslide Vulnerability Project policy-services agreement with Camoin Associates (not to exceed $90,000). See that meeting's summary for full detail. Moved together; no discussion.
Passed together by roll call, 6–0 (Councilor Rairdon absent). Moved by Gary Rairdon, seconded by Brian McCambridge.

Annual appointment and reappointment of Constables (process servers) for the Westbrook Housing Authority under Code of Ordinances §68-18. Constables may not carry weapons. Names per the packet: Erin Malloy, Hilary Elizabeth Mohn, Marc Montminy, Brittany Schmidtke, and Kristen Spiller.
Approved by roll call, 6–0, with Councilor Rairdon absent from the vote. Moved by Victor Chau, seconded by Amy Faulkingham.
Approves a major mass-gathering permit for Winterfest 2026 (Discover Downtown Westbrook). It is set for Saturday, March 7 at Riverbank Park, with expected attendance over 2,000.
Approved by unanimous roll call, 7–0. Moved by Brian McCambridge, seconded by Michael Shaughnessy.
Order 2026-14 — Q2 FY26 Unappropriated Funds Report
Routine acceptance of the quarterly report. It covers grants and donations under $5,000 that were accepted without advance Council approval, per Order 2021-121.
Approved by unanimous roll call, 7–0. Moved by Brian McCambridge, seconded by Michael Shaughnessy.
Order 2026-15 — GPCOG Memorandum of Understanding — PFAS Site Assessments

Authorizes the City to enter a Memorandum of Understanding with Greater Portland Council of Governments (GPCOG) for PFAS soil sampling at Fraser Field (489 Main St.), Warren Field (25 Stevens Ave.), and Westbrook High School (125 Stroudwater St.). It is funded entirely through GPCOG's USEPA Brownfields grant, at no cost to the City. It was first previewed at the Feb. 2 meeting; see §3 above.
Approved by unanimous roll call, 7–0. Moved by Michael Shaughnessy, seconded by Gary Rairdon.
Orders of the Day — Two Readings Required

Authorizes up to $1,915,000 in General Obligation Bonds (money the City borrows and repays over years) through the Maine Municipal Bond Bank. Of that, $915,000 is the City's share of the $1,665,000 Saco Street resurfacing project, with the Maine Department of Transportation providing $750,000. Another $1,000,000 is for the city-wide paving program. The City is paying off $1,005,000 in bonded debt this year.
Passed first reading, unanimous roll call, 7–0. Moved by Michael Shaughnessy, seconded by Gary Rairdon.
Order 2026-18 — Fire Department Donation — Thermal Imaging Cameras
Accepts an $8,000 donation from Maureen Strout. It also authorizes the purchase of two thermal imaging cameras from Industrial Protection Services, LLC (South Portland, ME) for $7,966.
Passed first reading, unanimous roll call, 7–0. Moved by Gary Rairdon, seconded by Michael Shaughnessy.
Order 2026-19 — Fire Department Donation — Furniture Replacement

Accepts a $10,000 donation from the estate of Blanche E. Kelley, given in memory of her brother, former Fire Chief Wilfred Rosenblad. It also authorizes $10,821.75 for Fire Department replacement furniture for the Public Safety Building and Station 3. The furniture is from Working Fire Furniture & Mattress Co., Inc. (Mebane, NC).
Passed first reading, unanimous roll call, 7–0. Moved by Michael Shaughnessy, seconded by Gary Rairdon.
Order 2026-20 — Emergency Fire Alarm Repair — Riverfront Parking Garage

Confirms $22,000 in emergency fire-alarm-system repairs at the Riverfront Parking Garage (Dana Court). The vendors are Corey Electric ($7,800), Pine State Fire and Security ($11,700), and Gilman Electric ($2,500). The repairs came after the roughly 20-year-old original system failed outright. They are funded through the garage's lease-funded reserve account, not City tax dollars.
Passed first reading, unanimous roll call, 7–0. Moved by Gary Rairdon, seconded by Michael Shaughnessy.
Order 2026-21 — 2026 Sewer Lining Program Bid Award

Awards the 2026 Sewer Lining Program bid to low bidder Insituform Technologies, LLC ($242,045). The work will line roughly 5,700 linear feet of sewer pipe across eight streets. It uses trenchless technology, with no street excavation. The goal is to reduce inflow/infiltration (groundwater and stormwater leaking into sewer pipes) into the sanitary sewer system.
Passed first reading, unanimous roll call, 7–0. Moved by Gary Rairdon, seconded by Victor Chau.
Order 2026-22 — Credere Associates Task Order A-100 — Brownfields Assessment Grant
Authorizes Task Order A-100 with Credere Associates ($210,000). Credere would serve as the City's qualified environmental professional for its $500,000 USEPA Brownfields Assessment Grant.
Passed first reading, unanimous roll call, 7–0. Moved by Michael Shaughnessy, seconded by Gary Rairdon.
Order 2026-23 — Summer Camp Field Trip Busing
Authorizes $12,369.76 to Dirigo Bus Lines (Gorham, ME) for six Westbrook Community Center Summer Camp field trips.
Passed first reading, unanimous roll call, 7–0. Moved by Brian McCambridge, seconded by Amy Faulkingham.

Councilor Rairdon noted the value of being able to conduct Council business remotely on a snow night. There were no referrals, no committee reports, and no executive session (a closed, private session allowed by state law for certain topics).
Motion to adjourn approved by unanimous roll call, 7–0. Moved by Gary Rairdon, seconded by Amy Faulkingham.

Quotes are lightly cleaned of filler words/false starts but not reworded. Reviewed by Gerald Doyon. A separate AI accuracy check then compared this summary against the transcript and agenda packet. Errors it found were corrected, and Gerald Doyon verified against the meeting video the points only the video could settle.
